justification: Fresh read, fetched directly this round rather than trusted from round 1. Microsoft's Fundamentals page (~2,922 words, the highest-authority result for the target query) states every fact this article states but has zero runnable code and zero worked leak scenarios -- it lists 'forgetting to free an object and causing a memory leak' as a problem GC 'eliminates' in its own Benefits section and then never once shows a case where a GC-managed program leaks anyway, which is precisely this article's content-plan angle (static-cache root, event-handler leak) and precisely what a reader who has just been told 'GC eliminates memory leaks' needs next. blog.elmah.io and techsyntax.net (both blog-tier, both rank for the query) confirmed the round-1 characterization on a second fetch: neither shows measured/executed output (techsyntax.net's examples are good-vs-bad style with no output at all; elmah.io's 'Gen 2 collections occurring every 3-5 seconds' is an invented illustrative number, not a run), neither cites a primary source inline, and between them they cover at most one of {IDisposable-vs-finalizer, weak references, event-leak mechanics} in any depth -- techsyntax.net has none of the three, elmah.io has finalizers but not weak references and only a one-line bullet on event leaks. This article runs all three, with real measured output and two original constructed scenarios (a permanent-root static cache, an event-subscriber leak fixed two ways). WebSearch quota was exhausted this session; I substituted quoted-phrase Bing fetches (a workable proxy for the same check) on five distinctive sentences ('Forty bytes of array length is the entire difference...', 'Two objects can hold references to each other and still both be garbage...', 'rides along with every full collection from the moment it is created', "the publisher's delegate list roots the subscriber", 'that cascade is the common path, not the only one') -- none returned a matching or near-matching indexed page, consistent with original writing. All four round-1 minors are fixed and none regressed: (1) the opening sentence now reads 'On the managed heap, a .NET program never calls `free`', correctly scoped so it no longer contradicts the article's own later `Marshal.FreeHGlobal` calls; (2) of six exercises, the second 'Find the bug' was reshaped into 'Prove it: make the check mean something' (the isalive-too-soon/isalive-proven pair), so the article now uses five of the brief's five named exercise forms across six exercises -- predict-the-output is the only form still used twice, which is normal variation, not a template, and I did not raise it as a fresh issue for that reason (see the one nit below, which is a different, narrower point); (3) the WeakReference-as-cache passage now quotes the source's actual caveat verbatim ('avoid using weak references as an automatic solution to memory management problems... instead, develop an effective caching policy') and correctly scopes the citation to the single-object tree-view example the source actually walks through, rather than claiming the source endorses WeakReference for the article's own many-item cache; (4) the CollectionCount 'at least that generation' claim is now split correctly -- the base definition is cited to the CollectionCount API page, and the 'at least' behavior is cited to Fundamentals' own 'collecting a generation means collecting objects in that generation and all its younger generations' line, which does support it. I read the rest of the article fresh rather than only checking the diff: sourcing is clean (all 11 front-matter sources are cited inline, none orphaned), structure has no boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion headings and no restated-heading summary (the closing section ends on an exercise, not a recap), the toolchain is disclosed once inline at the first machine-dependent number rather than as a stamped opening sentence, and no new unscoped absolute crept in during the fixes. This clears both blog-tier ranking results by a wide margin and does something the top-authority result does not attempt at all, which is close to the 10 anchor; it stays just under it because the exercise-label repetition ('Predict it:' twice) is real, if minor, and because matching a Bing-fetch proxy for five phrases is a weaker originality check than a full web search across the whole page.

issues.location: Exercise headings 'Predict it: which weak reference survives' (id=predict-roots) and 'Predict it: partial cleanup' (id=event-partial)
issues.problem: Both exercises open with the identical two words 'Predict it:'. This is a much smaller repetition than round 1's (which had two pairs of duplicated forms with no variety beyond them), and the brief only requires varying form across the five named shapes -- which this article now does, using all five across six exercises. But a reader who has just seen 'Predict it:' once will register the second instance as the same template, which is the kind of surface-level repetition an AdSense low-value-content pass is primed to notice even when the underlying content (weak references vs. event unsubscription) is unrelated.
issues.fixLooksLike: Retitle one of the two, e.g. 'Trace it: which weak reference survives' or fold a distinguishing detail into the heading itself ('Predict it, before you run it: partial cleanup'), so no two exercise headings on the page share their opening words.
